items.q: What is the best steampunk book to start with?
items.a: For a quick, gripping read, Mortal Engines, Leviathan or Boneshaker, in the gateway stage. For the foundations, Morlock Night or The Anubis Gates.

items.q: What are the best steampunk books for adults?
items.a: The founding novels and the literary stage: The Difference Engine, The Diamond Age, Perdido Street Station and Everfair.

items.q: What was the first steampunk novel?
items.a: The authorities disagree, and any single answer is an opinion. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction nominates Morlock Night (1979) as possibly the first significant steampunk novel.

items.q: Are there steampunk books for young readers?
items.a: Yes: Mortal Engines and Leviathan are the usual gateways, and Northern Lights is the guide's gentlest entry. See the teens list for more.

items.q: Did any steampunk novel win the Hugo Award?
items.a: Among the books here, The Diamond Age won the Hugo; Boneshaker was a finalist only. Girl Genius won the Hugo for best graphic story three years running.

items.a: Gaslamp fantasy keeps the setting and changes the engine. SF Crow's Nest puts the distinction briefly: steampunk likes machines, gaslamp likes mysteries; its examples of gaslamp are Anno Dracula and Soulless, and it says Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell is not st

items.q: The Smaller Cousins: Clockpunk, Solarpunk, Silkpunk
items.a: Clockpunk, according to SF Crow's Nest, reaches back before the steam age to Renaissance and early modern mechanics, with springs, gears and automata. We treat that as a soft source: no encyclopedia entry for the term was available to us.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is the difference between steampunk and dieselpunk?
items.a: Steampunk remixes an alternate nineteenth century powered by steam and clockwork, while dieselpunk remixes the interwar years and after, with Art Deco, pulp and noir. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction credits Lewis Pollak with coining dieselpunk in 2001.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is the difference between steampunk and cyberpunk?
items.a: Cyberpunk is 1980s science fiction of cybernetics, information networks and a streetwise attitude, and steampunk was named in imitation of it. The one looks forward from the 1980s; the other looks sideways at the nineteenth century.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is gaslamp fantasy, and how does it differ from steampunk?
items.a: It keeps the Victorian or Edwardian mood but lets magic and mystery do the work that machinery does in steampunk. One guide's shorthand is that steampunk likes machines and gaslamp likes mysteries.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is the difference between steampunk and solarpunk?
items.a: Solarpunk concerns renewable energy and ecological optimism, and the term dates from an anonymous 2008 blog post. Steampunk is a retrofuture of the nineteenth century.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: Is steampunk the same as Victorian?
items.a: No. Steampunk draws on Victorian and Edwardian settings, but it is an alternate or imagined version of them, and the American Heritage Dictionary also records the later sense of an aesthetic style.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is clockpunk?
items.a: A label for stories built on Renaissance or early modern mechanics such as springs, gears and automata, according to SF Crow's Nest. We rate that source as soft.
items.t: Steampunk vs Dieselpunk, Cyberpunk and Gaslamp: How to Tell Them Apart

items.q: What is steampunk in simple terms?
items.a: Fiction set in an alternate nineteenth century, usually Victorian England, with advanced machines run chiefly on steam; by extension, the brass-and-leather style inspired by it. It is both a kind of story and a look.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: What does steampunk mean in fashion?
items.a: It means Victorian and Edwardian clothing mixed with visible machinery: goggles, gears, corsets, waistcoats and tools. The dictionary's second sense, an aesthetic style inspired by the fiction, is the one that applies.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: Is steampunk a genre or an aesthetic?
items.a: Both, and scholars disagree about the emphasis. Garth Smith argues that it is better seen as an aesthetic that can be applied to any genre, while the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction treats it as a subgenre that later acquired a wider sense.

items.q: Is steampunk always Victorian?
items.a: No. The usual setting is Victorian or Edwardian England, but Tim Powers's The Anubis Gates is set in 1810, and Smith notes that much steampunk takes place in alternate worlds or the present.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: Where does the word steampunk come from?
items.a: From a 1987 letter by K. W. Jeter to Locus, modeled on the word cyberpunk. The full account is on the page on who coined steampunk.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: What is the difference between steampunk and dieselpunk?
items.a: Steampunk draws on the nineteenth century and its steam and clockwork; dieselpunk on the interwar years and after. See steampunk vs dieselpunk.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: Is steampunk still popular?
items.a: It is smaller than at its peak and still active: conventions continue, and scholars describe a diversifying subculture. There is no reliable count of fans.
items.t: What Is Steampunk? The Look, the Stories and Where the Word Came From

items.q: Who invented the word steampunk?
items.a: The novelist K. W. Jeter, in a letter printed in the April 1987 issue of Locus magazine. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction thinks it almost certain that he coined it himself.
items.t: Who Coined "Steampunk"? K. W. Jeter's 1987 Letter to Locus

items.q: What year was steampunk coined?
items.a: In 1987: the letter appeared in the Letters section of Locus that April. The novels it described reach back to 1979.
items.t: Who Coined "Steampunk"? K. W. Jeter's 1987 Letter to Locus

items.q: Why is it called steampunk?
items.a: It plays upon cyberpunk, the leading science-fiction label of the 1980s, with steam standing in for the computer. Jeter proposed a name founded on the technology of the Victorian era.
items.t: Who Coined "Steampunk"? K. W. Jeter's 1987 Letter to Locus

items.q: Was steampunk a joke?
items.a: In part. Perschon reads the "-punk" suffix as a playful nod to cyberpunk, and Dictionary.com also calls it partly in jest. The letter itself closes the suggestion with "perhaps".
items.t: Who Coined "Steampunk"? K. W. Jeter's 1987 Letter to Locus

items.q: What was the first steampunk book?
items.a: The authorities disagree: Morlock Night (1979), The Difference Engine (1990) and The Warlord of the Air (1971) each have their advocates. Any single answer is an opinion.

items.q: Who are Tim Powers and James Blaylock?
items.a: The two writers whom Jeter named alongside himself in the letter. Powers wrote The Anubis Gates (1983) and Blaylock wrote Homunculus (1986), both winners of the Philip K. Dick Award.
